Premiere: Jessica Sutta Takes Creative Control in ‘Don’t Take Much’ Music Video

Wednesday 7th October 2026
|In Music
|By FAULT Magazine

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 3:19
Instaread

Jessica Sutta puts her own vision at the centre of ‘Don’t Take Much’, pairing her latest dance-pop single with a video she has both directed and produced. Premiering on FAULT, the visual explores transformation through a shift from industrial darkness to a surreal landscape of colour and light. For Sutta, that transformation also has a personal dimension: stepping behind the camera means having a greater say in how her music, and she herself, are presented.

Co-written with Michael Warren and produced by Dave Audé, ‘Don’t Take Much’ introduces the direction of her forthcoming album. Its contemporary dance-pop framework connects with Sutta’s established club credentials, while a darker edge gives the new material its own identity. The song’s guiding idea is simplicity – peeling back the layers of a constructed persona and finding something more recognisable underneath.

That idea takes on a more elaborate form in the accompanying video. Shot in Nashville, it moves through a dark, seductive industrial setting before opening into a crystalline world of colour. Television imagery signals a return to familiar territory, while the playful “kidnapping” of a friend adds a mischievous interruption. The transition between these environments gives the video’s theme of alchemy a tangible shape: pressure, pain, and chaos becoming the raw materials for something powerful.

“Producing and directing has been a lifelong dream of mine. I’m constantly dream-weaving ideas in my head, so watching this one come to life, and knowing I trusted myself enough to make it happen, makes me incredibly proud.”

Jessica Sutta

The production stars Orion Solarion, and brings together choreography by Joy Spears, the dance talents of Laken Waters, and a cameo from Audé. Appearances from Sutta’s closest friends add a personal thread to the visual, grounding its heightened imagery in the relationships that support her.

Sutta’s background makes the move into directing a natural extension of her work as a performer. A dancer from childhood, she trained at Miami City Ballet and the New World School of the Arts before becoming captain of the Miami Heat dance team.
The Pussycat Dolls, who joined FAULT for a cover shoot and interview in 2020, subsequently took her onto international stages. Later, her solo career established a further foothold in dance music leading to her 2017 album, I Say Yes.

With ‘Don’t Take Much’, those experiences feed into a project whose authorship extends beyond the recording studio. Sutta is shaping the choreography, imagery, and emotional context around the song as well as the music itself. The result marks a new chapter defined by the freedom to decide how she wants to be seen.
